overview: This file documents an extended 1946–47 State Department dispute over French demands for approximately $37.3 million in gold earmarked in Tokyo by wartime Japan for the Saigon branch of the Bank of Indochina. Officials agreed that earmarking might have transferred legal title but disagreed sharply over whether the transactions represented legitimate payment, compensation extracted under duress, or a reward for Vichy French collaboration with Japan. The discussions compare the French claim with larger Siamese gold credits, Japanese reparations and restitution policy, occupation financing, European precedents for monetary gold, and the political status of French Indochina and Siam during the war. The file ends without a definitive settlement, with proposals ranging from outright refusal, through partial release based on the date of earmarking, to provisional delivery subject to review by the Far Eastern Commission.

subfiles.title: Martin memorandum on the French request for earmarked gold
subfiles.to: Alwyn V. Freeman, Office of the Legal Adviser
subfiles.about: Reports the initial French presentation and requests legal and political advice on releasing gold earmarked in Japan for the Saigon branch of the Bank of Indochina.
subfiles.summary: French representatives Robert Douteau and Marcel Clement described 2,283 bars weighing 33,056,813.6 grams and worth about $37.31 million, allegedly earmarked as payment for Indochinese imports and Japanese military expenditures. They argued that the claim fell outside both restitution and reparations because the gold had not been confiscated and represented payment rather than spoliation. The memorandum also notes more than one billion yen in related balances, comparable Japanese earmarking for Siam, and the need for expedited interdepartmental consultation.

subfiles.title: Freeman legal opinion on the French gold claim
subfiles.from: Alwyn V. Freeman, Office of the Legal Adviser
subfiles.about: Assesses whether Japanese earmarking transferred legal title to the French and whether broader policy considerations nevertheless justified withholding the gold.
subfiles.summary: Freeman concludes that existing Far Eastern Commission restitution directives do not cover the earmarked gold and identifies the decisive legal question as whether earmarking effected a transfer of property. Treasury advice indicated that normal banking practice treated segregated earmarked bars as the recipient central bank's physical property. Although this gave France a substantial legal case, Freeman argued that the Vichy regime's collaboration, the anti-Allied origin of the transactions, and precedent concerning puppet-government assets might justify refusing release on policy grounds.

subfiles.title: Robinson memorandum requesting political comment on French gold
subfiles.to: John Carter Vincent, FE; H. Freeman Matthews, EUR
subfiles.about: Solicits Far Eastern and European political views on the French demand for release of $37.3 million in gold.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum reviews the estimated amounts and dates of earmarking and reports that SCAP had been asked to obtain detailed Japanese records. JK tentatively favored treating only gold earmarked before the May 1941 occupation of French Indochina as the proceeds of normal commerce, with later gold left to reparations settlement. It also records prospective French claims to approximately 1.3 billion yen and a smaller dollar balance in the Yokohama Specie Bank.

subfiles.title: Metzger memorandum on gold found at the German Legation in China
subfiles.about: Recommends returning gold found at the German Legation to China while asking China to hold it for IARA if its German origin is established.
subfiles.summary: Metzger argues that China was not a party to the IARA Gold Resolution and that the resolution was probably designed for territories under German occupation or influence rather than the Far East. Because the quantity was small and came into American custody under unusual circumstances, he favored inviting Chinese accession to the resolution instead of applying it mechanically.

subfiles.title: Martin memorandum on French wartime status and the gold claim
subfiles.to: John Carter Vincent, FE; H. Freeman Matthews, EUR
subfiles.about: Frames the gold and reparations questions around the wartime status of French authorities in Indochina.
subfiles.summary: Martin considers four possible descriptions of the Indochinese administration—neutral, puppet, belligerent, or collaborative—and explains the consequences of each for ownership of the gold. JK proposes treating the administration as collaborative and denying any claim to the gold earmarked between November 1941 and May 1943. For reparations, Martin suggests arguing that belligerency applicable to Indochina began no earlier than October 1944, when the United States recognized de Gaulle's sovereignty there.

subfiles.title: Vincent memorandum comparing French Indochinese and Siamese gold
subfiles.about: Argues that the United States should apply the same policy to French Indochinese and Siamese gold credits established while their governments aided Japan.
subfiles.summary: Vincent states that both governments supplied goods, currency, and facilities to Japanese forces under duress, French Indochina from August 30, 1940 to March 9, 1945 and Siam from December 8, 1941 to May 25, 1945. He recommends forfeiting credits created during those periods while releasing credits established before or afterward. If France nevertheless obtained all its credits as legal successor, Vincent argued that Siam should receive identical treatment.

subfiles.title: Annex A: wartime status of French Indochina
subfiles.about: Provides a chronology supporting the view that French Indochina collaborated under duress from August 1940 and became belligerent against Japan only in March 1945.
subfiles.summary: The annex recounts the closing of the Tonkin border, the August 30, 1940 agreement recognizing Japanese predominance, subsequent military-access agreements, and the September fighting at the border, Haiphong, and Doson. It then reviews Japanese economic privileges, the May 1941 commercial agreement, and the July 1941 Vichy protocol for political and military cooperation. FE concludes that the August 30 agreement marked the start of collaboration and that belligerent status did not apply until Japan displaced the French administration on March 9, 1945.

subfiles.title: Annex B: wartime status of Siam
subfiles.about: Reviews Siam's alliance and material assistance to Japan and the emergence of a resistance movement prepared to act against the Japanese in 1945.
subfiles.summary: The annex describes Siam's December 8, 1941 agreement under duress, the December 21 alliance with Japan, the January 1942 declarations of war, and subsequent provision of baht, goods, and facilities. It recounts consultations involving Seni Pramoj and Regent Pridi Banomyong about openly joining the Allies. The annex concludes that the resistance was ready to act by May 25, 1945 but deferred action at the request of the Supreme Allied Commander and the Acting Secretary of State.

subfiles.title: Reber memorandum on the starting date for forfeiture
subfiles.to: H. Freeman Matthews, EUR; John Carter Vincent, FE
subfiles.about: Concurs with forfeiting wartime gold credits but questions whether Japan could legally be called an enemy before December 1941.
subfiles.summary: Reber accepts Vincent's basic rule that credits established while French Indochina or Siam aided Japanese aggression should be forfeited. He recommends, however, that the relevant French Indochinese period begin on December 8, 1941 rather than August 30, 1940 because the United States was not yet at war with Japan before December 1941.

subfiles.title: Hilldring recommendation to treat French gold as reparations
subfiles.about: Recommends rejecting immediate French ownership claims and treating the earmarked gold solely as a reparations matter.
subfiles.summary: Hilldring reports the French ambassador's request for $37.3 million and argues that the gold arose from resources taken during occupation. Recognition would invite an analogous Siamese claim for $43.7 million, diminish liquid assets available for Japanese foreign trade, and give France preferential compensation over other occupied areas. Despite acknowledging a substantial legal basis for France, he recommends a negative reply and submits a proposed draft note.

subfiles.title: Ness memorandum supporting release of the French gold
subfiles.to: Willard L. Thorp, A-T; John H. Hilldring, A-H
subfiles.about: Opposes JK's recommendation and urges American support for releasing the earmarked gold to France.
subfiles.summary: Ness proposes action through the Far Eastern Commission or a direct SCAP instruction, invoking the inviolability of lawful international transfers of monetary gold. He cites European policy separating gold restitution from reparations and the intended return of German gold found in Japan to the European gold pool. He also argues that denial would not benefit reparations claimants because American proposals already contemplated using Japanese gold for occupation costs and foreign-trade financing.

subfiles.title: Ness note on Treasury opposition
subfiles.to: Willard L. Thorp, A-T; John H. Hilldring, A-H
subfiles.about: Reports that the Treasury Department would strongly oppose any refusal to release the Indochinese gold.
subfiles.summary: This brief follow-up supplements Ness's July 17 memorandum. It emphasizes that Treasury would strenuously resist a decision withholding the gold from the French Union.

subfiles.title: Vincent memorandum proposing a chronological compromise
subfiles.to: Willard L. Thorp, A-T; John H. Hilldring, A-H
subfiles.about: Proposes releasing only French and Siamese gold earmarked before the countries entered periods of collaboration with Japan.
subfiles.summary: Vincent endorses the JK memorandum and rejects OFD's approach, arguing that actual collaboration at the time of earmarking should control the decision. His preferred dates would withhold French Indochinese gold from August 30, 1940 and Siamese gold from December 8, 1941, though he accepts December 8, 1941 as a compromise date for Indochina. The compromise would release $12 million to France and $8 million to Siam while treating later credits as reparations matters.

subfiles.title: Surrey legal comments on the Indochinese gold
subfiles.from: W. S. Surrey, Office of the Legal Adviser
subfiles.about: Concludes that the ultimate issue is political but that France probably has the stronger legal claim to the earmarked gold.
subfiles.summary: Surrey argues that duress did not prevent French Indochina from affirming the transactions and claiming the promised compensation, and that legal earmarking could be equivalent to physical shipment. He finds no decisive European precedent and regards the choice as political rather than compelled by law. If the gold were returned, he suggests discussing the decision alongside French-Italian disagreements over Italian participation in Swiss looted-gold distributions.

subfiles.title: War Department transmittal of SCAP report on Thai gold
subfiles.from: Ray J. Lane for Major General Daniel Noce, War Department Civil Affairs Division
subfiles.to: John H. Hilldring, Assistant Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Transmits SCAP's response concerning the circumstances, quantity, identification, and status of gold earmarked for Siamese account.
subfiles.summary: The letter responds to a June 24 State Department cable requesting information about Japanese gold earmarked for Siam. Lane states that SCAP had supplied the requested information and forwards it as a report entitled “Report of Gold in Japan Earmarked for Thailand.” The listed enclosure itself is not reproduced in the OCR file.

subfiles.title: McGuire memorandum opposing release to France
subfiles.about: Forcefully rejects OFD's release recommendation and argues that the gold represented a Japanese reward for Vichy collaboration.
subfiles.summary: McGuire depicts the earmarking system as preferential compensation for French Indochina and Siam, contrasting it with the restricted yen or uncompensated seizures imposed on territories that resisted Japan. He argues that releasing the gold would privilege collaborators over other reparations claimants and uses a hypothetical Soviet expansion in Europe to warn against declaring gold transactions inviolable regardless of circumstances. McGuire recommends compensating France through ordinary reparations procedures, using the gold and yen credits as evidence of losses, and asks OFD to withdraw its July 17 memorandum. He allows that a compromise might release pre-Pearl Harbor credits, although he doubts China would accept even that concession.

subfiles.title: Saltzman memorandum on referral to the Far Eastern Commission
subfiles.to: Robert A. Lovett, Under Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Recommends referring the French claim to the Far Eastern Commission or making any urgent delivery provisional and reversible.
subfiles.summary: Saltzman favors FEC consideration unless immediate assistance to France is judged exceptionally important. In that event, he suggests recognizing prima facie French title and delivering the gold only after France agrees to return an equivalent amount if a competent body later rules against it. He distinguishes Siam because its enemy status toward countries represented by SCAP might support cancellation of the transaction or seizure as war booty.

interest: The file is especially valuable for exposing an unresolved conflict among State Department bureaus, the Legal Adviser, Treasury, and occupation authorities over the relationship between technical legal title and the moral-political consequences of wartime collaboration. Its detailed annexes reconstruct French Indochinese and Siamese relations with Japan, while the successive memoranda show officials testing occupation dates, belligerency, duress, reparations equality, European gold precedents, and even early Cold War analogies. The unusually candid language about Vichy collaboration, colonial claims, China, and rewards for resistance makes the bundle useful for studying both postwar economic diplomacy and American judgments about legitimacy in former Japanese-occupied territories.
